text: Jóhanna Sigurðardóttir, born on 4 October 1942 in Reykjavík, is an Icelandic politician who served as prime minister from 2009 to 2013. She was a member of the Althing (Iceland's parliament) for the Reykjavík constituencies from 1978 to 2013, winning re-election eight times. She studied at the Commercial College of Iceland and graduated in 1960 with a commercial diploma. From 1962 to 1971, she worked as a flight attendant with Icelandic Airlines, and from 1971 to 1978 as an office manager. She was active in trade unions, presiding over the Icelandic Cabin Crew Association and the Association of Former Stewardesses, and serving on the Board of the Commercial Workers' Union from 1976 to 1983. Elected to the Althing in 1978 on the Social Democratic Party list, she served as deputy speaker in 1979 and from 1983 to 1984, and was elected vice-chairperson of the Social Democratic Party in 1984, holding the position until 1993. She served as Minister of Social Affairs and Social Security from 1987 to 1994 and again from 2007 to 2009. In 1994, after losing the leadership bid for the Social Democratic Party, she declared "Minn tími mun koma!" ("My time will come!"), a phrase that became widely known in Iceland. She then left the party and founded the National Awakening (Þjóðvaki), which received 7.1% of the vote and four seats in the 1995 election, before all MPs joined the Social Democratic Party in 1996. In the 1999 election, National Awakening ran with the Social Democratic Alliance, and the parties officially merged in 2000. From 1994 to 2003, she was an opposition member in the Althing, serving on various committees. After the 2003 elections, she was re-elected deputy speaker from the Reykjavík South constituency. In the 2007 elections, from the Reykjavík North constituency, she returned to government as Minister of Social Affairs and Social Security with the Social Democratic Alliance and the Independence Party. On 26 January 2009, Prime Minister Geir Haarde resigned following the 2008 financial crisis, and President Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson asked the Social Democratic Alliance and the Left-Green Movement to form a new government. Jóhanna was proposed as prime minister due to her public popularity and strong relations with the Left-Green Movement; a Capacent Gallup poll in December 2008 found 73% approval of her actions, the highest among cabinet members, with her approval ratings improving over 2008. The new government required support from the Progressive Party, and after negotiations ending on 31 January, the cabinet was appointed on 1 February 2009. A parliamentary election on 25 April 2009 followed the Kitchenware Revolution protests, resulting in the Social Democratic Alliance and the Left-Green Movement gaining overall majority seats, with the Progressive Party and the new Citizens' Movement also gaining seats, while the Independence Party lost support and seats. On 10 May 2009, Jóhanna remained prime minister in the new government. During her tenure, several referendums were held on Icesave bank debts; the first on 6 March 2010, followed by a second on 9 April 2011, both resulting in "no" votes. After the second referendum failed, the British and Dutch governments stated they would take the case to European courts. On 28 September 2010, the Althing voted 33–30 to indict former prime minister Geir Haarde on charges of negligence, but not other ministers, in a case heard by the Landsdómur, a special court established in 1905. The left coalition government, comprising the Social Democratic Alliance, the Left-Green Movement, the Progressive Party, and the Liberal Party, agreed to convene a constitutional assembly inspired by citizen protests. On 4 November 2009, a bill was introduced to involve citizens in drafting a new constitution. A National Forum, Þjóðfundur 2009, was held on 14 November 2009 at Laugardalshöll in Reykjavík, with 1,200 randomly selected participants from the national registry. On 16 June 2010, the Constitutional Act was passed by parliament, establishing a new Forum 2010 with a seven-member Constitutional Committee overseeing the process and the Anthill group organizing it. On 26 October 2010, 25 non-partisan citizens were elected to a Constitutional Council, though the Supreme Court invalidated the election results on 25 January 2011 due to procedural faults; the parliament upheld the process and accepted the candidates as part of the council. On 29 July 2011, the draft constitution was presented to parliament, which voted on 24 May 2012 to organize an advisory referendum on the proposal by 20 October 2012, with 35 in favor and 15 against, the only opposition coming from the former governing Independence Party. A proposed referendum to end Iceland's accession talks with the European Union was rejected, with 34 votes against and 25 in favor. In 2010, her government banned strip clubs, payments for nudity in restaurants, and other forms of employer profit from employee nudity—making it the first such ban in a Western democratic country. Jóhanna stated that the Nordic countries were leading in women's equality, recognizing women as equal citizens. Julie Bindel of The Guardian called Iceland the most feminist country in the world. In 2012, when asked about the most important gender-based issue, she said it was "to fight the pay gap between men and women." She married Þorvaldur Steinar Jóhannesson in 1970 and had two sons, Sigurður Egill Þorvaldsson (born 1972) and Davíð Steinar Þorvaldsson (born 1977). After divorcing in 1987, she entered a civil union with Jónína Leósdóttir (born 1954) in 2002. When same-sex marriage was legalized in Iceland in 2010, Jóhanna and Jónína converted their civil union into a marriage, becoming one of the first same-sex married couples in the country. In 2017, she published a biography titled Minn tími ("My Time"), covering the period from the 2008 financial crisis through the protests, emergency elections, and the recovery under the left-wing government.
